yourBaby: Eyelids can open partway, and your baby can blink. Eyelashes are in.
The brain and nervous system can help steady body temperature and start practice breathing movements.
Lungs are making surfactant, which helps them expand. Those practice breaths may show up on a scan.
Hearing is sharpening. Your baby may recognize your voice and startle at a loud sound.
Hiccups are common as the diaphragm practices.
About 10 inches (25 cm) from crown to rump and about 2¼ pounds (1 kg). Often compared with a large eggplant.
Your baby may still be breech. Most turn head-down closer to birth.
yourBody: The third trimester starts, and antenatal visits often become more frequent.
Backache, leg cramps, heartburn, and swelling in the hands or feet are common.
The growing uterus can make sitting, standing, and sleeping less comfortable.
suggestionsThisWeek: Sleep on your side from now on. If you wake on your back, roll onto your side.
Take off tight jewelry and rest with your feet up when swelling shows up.
Notice your baby's usual movement pattern each day. Call your midwife or doctor the same day if movements slow or change.
You may be offered a glucose test for gestational diabetes, and anti-D if your blood type is Rh negative.
Talk or sing to your baby. A childbirth class and a first list for your birth bag are useful if you have not started them.

yourBaby: Your baby can kick, stretch, and make grasping movements.
Growth is still fast, and your baby is about a third of a typical full-term size.
Organs are formed and most are working. Lungs practice a steadier breathing rhythm.
Red blood cells are forming in the bone marrow.
Eyelids can open and eyelashes have grown. Sight is still maturing, and the head is growing to make room for the brain.
Often compared with a butternut squash.
yourBody: The uterus presses on the diaphragm, stomach, and other organs, so shortness of breath and indigestion can show up.
Tiredness is common, and a full night of sleep is harder.
If you have asthma, symptoms can change in pregnancy. Keep the plan your clinician has already given you.
suggestionsThisWeek: Rest earlier in the evening if you need to, and keep side-sleeping.
Tell your clinician if breathlessness feels severe, not just occasional.
Draft a birth plan: place of birth, support people, positions, and pain-relief preferences. Treat it as a guide you can change.

yourBaby: Eyes can open wide. Hair on the head may be fuller, while fine body hair (lanugo) starts to thin.
Fat stores are filling in, so the skin looks smoother and less wrinkled.
Toenails are forming, and reflexes include sucking a thumb or fingers.
Red blood cells continue to form in the bone marrow.
About 10½ inches (27 cm) from crown to rump and nearly 3 pounds (1.3 kg). Often compared with a large cabbage.
Amniotic fluid is still plentiful, though your baby will take more of that space as they grow.
yourBody: Stretching ligaments can make long sitting or standing ache. Backache is common.
Blood volume is much higher. Blood pressure is checked at visits because it can rise without obvious symptoms.
High blood pressure can also be a sign of pre-eclampsia, which is why routine checks matter.
suggestionsThisWeek: Keep gentle movement on most days, such as walking or swimming, if your clinician agrees. Skip high-impact bouncing and long stretches flat on your back.
Lift carefully. Flat shoes, a support cushion, or a maternity belt can ease your back.
Keep tracking movements, and contact your care team the same day if the pattern changes.
Go to blood-pressure checks even when you feel well.

yourBaby: Most major development is finished. This is a stretch of fast weight gain.
Fat is building under the skin and rounding the arms and legs.
Your baby can turn the head from side to side, open the eyes, and focus.
Hearing reaches sounds outside the uterus, and a loud noise can cause a startle.
Often compared with a coconut.
yourBody: Low energy is common.
Emotions can feel stronger, from hormones, broken sleep, or thoughts about becoming a parent.
Breasts may leak more. That is expected for many people.
suggestionsThisWeek: Talk to your baby or play music you like.
Breast pads can make leaking more comfortable.
If sadness, anxiety, or stress feels heavy, tell your midwife or doctor. Mood changes in pregnancy are common, and help is available.
Arrange a rear-facing infant car seat that meets your local safety standard, and have it fitted before the due date.

yourBaby: Toenails are visible, and lanugo starts to shed.
Weight has risen quickly and will usually increase faster than length. A large share of birth weight is still ahead.
About 11 inches (28 cm) from crown to rump and about 3¾ pounds (1.7 kg). Often compared with a papaya.
Most babies are head-down. Some stay breech into the last month.
Movements should continue in your baby's usual pattern, even in a tighter space.
yourBody: There is more amniotic fluid, and the bump is growing quickly.
Pelvic pain can make walking harder.
Your navel may flatten or stick out.
suggestionsThisWeek: Ask about physiotherapy if pelvic pain limits how you move.
Remove navel jewelry if a piercing is stretched.
Know the signs that need same-day care: regular contractions, waters breaking, bleeding, a mucus show, or a sudden change in movement.
Ask whether whooping cough and seasonal flu vaccines are recommended for you now.

yourBaby: Pupils can change size in response to light.
Bones are hardening, but the skull plates stay soft and unfused so the head can mold in the birth canal.
Lungs keep maturing and making surfactant.
The brain and nervous system are well developed. Sucking and swallowing are present, though not fully coordinated yet.
Iron is being stored in the liver for the early months after birth.
Often compared with a pineapple.
yourBody: Leg cramps, backache, heartburn, and swelling of the feet and legs often increase.
The baby's weight can press on the bladder and bowel, so frequent peeing, leaking, or hemorrhoids can appear.
suggestionsThisWeek: Do pelvic-floor exercises daily.
Contact your clinician promptly if swelling suddenly worsens, is there first thing in the morning, or involves the face or hands.
Learn your baby's own rhythm, including quiet times while you are moving and active spells at night. A clear change needs a same-day call.

yourBaby: Fingernails have reached the fingertips.
The immune system, central nervous system, and lungs are maturing.
Skull bones are harder but still not fused. Soft spots (fontanelles) let the plates overlap in birth and leave room for the brain to grow.
About 12 inches (30 cm) from crown to rump and more than 4½ pounds (2.1 kg). Often compared with a cantaloupe.
A baby born around now is still preterm. With no other health problems, many do well with medical care.
yourBody: Tiredness, aches, and broken sleep often continue.
Pain at the top of the legs can come from stretching ligaments.
How much weight you gain depends on your weight before pregnancy. Your clinician can talk through a range that fits you.
suggestionsThisWeek: Rest, keep meals regular, and continue gentle movement plus pelvic-floor exercises.
Tell your midwife or doctor if leg or pelvic pain is severe.
If your blood type is Rh negative, a second anti-D injection is often offered around 34 to 36 weeks, and also after a bleed. Ask at your next visit.

yourBaby: Your baby fills most of the amniotic sac and has less room, but should still stretch, roll, and wiggle in the usual pattern.
Kidneys are mature. Your baby swallows amniotic fluid and passes it back as urine. The liver can handle some waste.
Legs are often tucked toward the chest, and position can still change.
Often compared with a honeydew melon.
yourBody: Braxton Hicks tightenings can come every 10 to 20 minutes. They often ease when you change position.
Pre-eclampsia is watched for in late pregnancy, usually through blood pressure and urine checks.
suggestionsThisWeek: Practice tightenings fade with a position change. Call if contractions grow stronger, longer, or closer, feel worse when you walk, or come with pelvic or back pain. Labor now would be preterm.
Seek care the same day for a severe headache, tummy pain, blurry vision, or sudden swelling of the hands or feet.
If your baby is still breech in the next week or two, your clinician may discuss a turning procedure (external cephalic version).
Start a hospital or birth bag a couple of weeks ahead.

yourBaby: Skin is smoothing as fat builds, and the limbs look chubbier. Your baby is gaining about an ounce a day.
Most of the lanugo and the waxy vernix that coated the skin are shedding.
Many babies are head-down. In a first pregnancy, the head may settle into the pelvis (engagement).
Often compared with a head of romaine lettuce.
The usual movement pattern should continue until birth.
yourBody: The uterus reaches toward the ribcage. If the head engages, the bump may sit a little lower.
You may feel more pelvic pressure, need the toilet more often, and breathe a bit more easily once the baby drops.
Vaginal discharge often increases.
suggestionsThisWeek: Tell your clinician if discharge smells strong, looks green or brown, or makes you itchy or sore.
If your baby is not head-down, ask about options. Turning is often discussed around week 37.
You may be offered a group B strep test. Ask what a positive result would mean for labor.
Call the same day if movements change.

yourBaby: Early term begins. The grip is firm and the lungs can work, but lungs and brain keep maturing. Full term is 39 weeks.
The gut holds sticky meconium, which becomes the first poo. Digestion keeps maturing long after birth.
The head may move down into the pelvis to get ready for birth.
Often compared with a bunch of Swiss chard.
The usual movement pattern should continue, including during labor.
yourBody: When the head engages, the upper belly can feel a little easier and the pelvis fuller. This is more common in a first pregnancy.
Colostrum may leak.
Early labor hints can appear any time from now through 42 weeks: period-like cramps, backache, loose stools, a mucus show, or waters breaking. The day itself is hard to predict.
suggestionsThisWeek: Ask your clinician before expressing and storing colostrum. Breast pads can help if leaking bothers you.
If you are still working, this is a common week to finish. Plan simple meals and rest for the first days at home.
There is no reliable way to predict when labor will start, even if you have given birth before.

yourBaby: Toenails reach the tips of the toes, and most lanugo is gone. A little vernix may still coat the skin.
Measurements around the head and the belly are often similar.
Weight varies widely, often around 6½ pounds (2.9 kg), and some babies are closer to 9 pounds (4 kg).
Eye color at birth is not final. The irises can keep changing for months.
Often compared with a small watermelon.
If meconium is released into the amniotic fluid, the fluid can look green and the baby is watched more closely.
yourBody: Labor can start any time from now until 42 weeks.
You may feel pelvic pressure, cramps, backache, loose stools, a mucus show, or waters breaking as a trickle or a gush.
Some people get a burst of energy and want to prepare the house.
suggestionsThisWeek: Rest even during a nesting urge, and avoid overdoing it.
Know who to call, when to leave, and how you will get there. Do not drive yourself in labor.
Active labor is usually strong, regular contractions that each last about a minute. Call your midwife or doctor when you think it has started.

yourBaby: Full term. The body is essentially complete, and fat is still being added to help with warmth after birth.
The chest is broader. The brain is growing quickly, so the head is a large share of body weight.
Weight gain may slow. Creamy vernix may still cover the skin.
Often compared with a pumpkin.
yourBody: The cervix softens, thins, and opens toward about 10 cm.
A mucus show can appear, sometimes streaked with a little old blood. Heavier bleeding needs a call right away.
The placenta has grown along with your baby. Birthing it is the third stage of labor, and you can talk through how you prefer that to be managed.
suggestionsThisWeek: Extra scans are uncommon now unless there is a reason, such as diabetes, high blood pressure, more than one baby, or a movement concern.
In early labor, rest at home if your clinician has said that is right for you. Go in when contractions are strong and about 3 to 5 minutes apart, or sooner if you are not coping.
Pack clothes, toiletries, and pads for you, plus clothes and nappies for the baby.

yourBaby: A common size is about 14 inches (36 cm) from crown to rump and about 7½ pounds (3.4 kg). Healthy term babies also range widely, often about 6½ to 9 pounds (2.9 to 4.2 kg).
Often compared with a watermelon.
Bones are developed, but the skull plates stay flexible so the head can pass through the birth canal. A briefly pointed shape after birth is common.
Movements still matter through the end of pregnancy and into labor.
yourBody: Only a small share of babies arrive on the due date. The date is an estimate, and later ovulation can shift it.
Going past the date is common and is usually watched closely.
If the pregnancy goes well beyond the date, or if there is a health concern, your clinician may discuss inducing labor.
suggestionsThisWeek: Decisions about induction belong in a conversation with your care team.
Call the same day if the movement pattern changes.
After birth you will usually be offered newborn checks such as a heel-prick screen, vitamin K, a hepatitis B vaccination, and a hearing test. You can ask about each one beforehand.
